analogy.p: A sculptor starts with a block of stone (the varied population) and removes pieces over many sessions until the shape they want remains. Each generation the breeder removes unwanted forms by not allowing them to breed, until the population looks the way the breeder wants. It maps the idea that variation is the raw material and humans decide what is kept. It breaks down because a sculptor can't un-remove stone: if breeders remove too much variation they may lose alleles forever, and the sculptor works with one block while a population is made of living individuals that also face disease and the environment.
analogy.t: Sculpting a statue from a block

bullets: Definition to learn: 'the process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics'.
The chosen characteristic must be **inherited**: breeding a fat cow does not help if the fatness was caused only by feeding.
The selecting agent is **humans**; for natural selection the selecting agent is the **environment**.
The characteristic chosen is useful or attractive to **people**, not necessarily to the survival of the organism in the wild.
It is a form of **evolution** driven by humans, speeding up change in the frequency of chosen alleles.
It does **not** involve changing genes directly; it uses the **natural variation** already present. This is the key difference from genetic engineering.
Used in both plants and animals, and for both food production and pets or ornamental use.
core.p: **Selective breeding** (also called **artificial selection**) is the process by which **humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics**. Instead of the environment deciding which individuals reproduce, **people choose** the parents. Humans have used selective breeding for **thousands of years** to produce the crops, farm animals and pets we have today. It works because the chosen characteristics are controlled by **alleles**, which are passed from parents to offspring.

bullets: Step 1: **Decide on the desired characteristic** (for example high milk yield or disease resistance).
Step 2: From a population showing variation, **select the individuals with that characteristic** as parents.
Step 3: **Breed them together** (sexual reproduction mixes the alleles).
Step 4: From the offspring, **select those with the desired characteristic most strongly developed**.
Step 5: **Breed these** together.
Step 6: **Repeat over many generations** until all the offspring show the characteristic well.
Mark-scheme words: 'select', 'breed', 'offspring', 'repeat', 'over many generations'.
Crucially, you must **choose parents each generation**; choosing once is not enough.
core.p: Selective breeding follows a repeating cycle that must be written in order. You begin with a **mixed population** showing variation, choose the individuals with the characteristic you want, breed them, then choose the best of their offspring and repeat. Each generation, the proportion of the population with the desired alleles rises. After **many generations** the population has the trait strongly. The process is slow because the improvement is gradual and the animals or plants must reach breeding age each time.

bullets: **Disease resistance in food crops**, so less pesticide and fewer lost harvests.
**Larger fruit** or more fruit per plant gives higher yield and profit.
**Better taste**, longer shelf life, or uniform size for supermarkets.
**Drought resistance** or faster ripening for different climates.
**Flowers** with large, unusual or scented blooms, bred for gardens.
Method: choose plants with the best feature, cross-pollinate them, grow the seeds, choose the best seedlings, repeat.
Plants usually have shorter generation times than large animals, so progress can be quicker.
Link: the **gene pool** of wild relatives is a valuable source of alleles for disease resistance.
core.p: Plants are selectively bred to give crops with better properties, such as **disease resistance**, **larger or better-tasting fruit**, **higher yield**, and **resistance to drought or cold**. Ornamental plants are bred for **large or unusual flowers**, colour or scent. The wild cabbage plant is a famous case: from one wild species, farmers selected for different features to produce cabbage (large terminal bud), kale (leaves), broccoli and cauliflower (flowers), Brussels sprouts (side buds) and kohlrabi (swollen stem).

bullets: **Cattle** for high milk yield or high meat yield.
**Chickens** for large numbers of eggs or fast growth.
**Domestic dogs** for a **gentle nature**, herding ability, or appearance.
**Horses** for speed or strength.
**Sheep** for the quality and amount of wool, or disease resistance.
For example, to increase milk yield, a farmer keeps the best milk-producing cows and uses a bull whose female relatives produced a lot of milk, then repeats with the best daughters.
The characteristic must have a **genetic** basis; milk yield is also affected by feed, so farmers must consider that.
Keeping records of each animal's performance helps choose the best parents.
core.p: Animals are bred for characteristics useful to people. Farm animals are bred for **more meat**, **more milk**, **more eggs** or **wool**. Dogs and horses are bred for features such as a **gentle nature** or **speed**. The same step-by-step cycle is used: choose the males and females with the best characteristic, breed them, then choose the best offspring. Because animals take longer to mature and have fewer offspring, results are slower than for plants.

bullets: Many characteristics are controlled by **several genes**, so progress may need many generations.
Breeding two individuals with a **dominant** trait may not guarantee offspring with that trait if both are heterozygous; offspring need to be tested.
Alleles for **recessive** traits are only seen if the offspring inherit two copies, so breeders must be careful.
Selection reduces variation for the chosen trait: over time the **gene pool** shrinks.
Chance mutations may add useful new alleles that breeders can select.
Link: inheritance diagrams (Punnett squares) can predict the chance of offspring showing a trait.
Evidence that it works: modern farm breeds produce far more milk, meat or grain than their wild ancestors.
core.h: Why it works: alleles, variation and inheritance
core.p: Selective breeding works because there is **variation** in a population and that variation is partly **genetic**. By breeding together only individuals with the wanted **alleles**, the **frequency of these alleles** in the next generation is higher. Repeating this concentrates the alleles until nearly all offspring have them. If there were no genetic variation, there would be nothing to select, which is why **mutation** and **sexual reproduction** (the sources of variation) are so important.

bullets: Natural selection: **environment** selects; selective breeding: **humans** select.
Natural selection favours **survival and breeding success**; selective breeding favours **human wants**.
Natural selection is usually **slow**; selective breeding is faster because only chosen individuals breed.
Natural selection tends to keep variation; selective breeding tends to **reduce variation**.
Bred organisms may not survive well without human care, for example some dog breeds with extreme features.
Both are examples of how the frequency of alleles changes over **many generations**.
Exam tip: when comparing, use 'whereas' or 'but' so that both sides are in the same sentence.
core.h: Selective breeding compared with natural selection
core.p: Both processes change the frequency of alleles in a population and need variation, inheritance and repeated generations. The key difference is **what does the selecting** and **what is selected for**. In natural selection, the environment favours characteristics that help **survival and reproduction**. In selective breeding, humans choose characteristics that are **useful or attractive to people**, even if they would reduce survival in the wild.

bullets: Inbreeding = 'breeding of closely related individuals'.
It **reduces the size of the gene pool** (fewer different alleles).
Harmful recessive alleles, normally hidden in carriers, are more likely to be paired, so **inherited disorders** appear.
Examples: some pedigree dog breeds suffer from joint problems, and short-nosed breeds can have breathing difficulties.
Inbreeding can reduce **fertility** and increase the risk of early death.
It also lowers the ability of the population to cope with new diseases or environmental change.
Solution: breeders can bring in unrelated individuals to widen the gene pool, with careful record keeping.
Ethical issue: is it acceptable to breed animals with features that cause suffering?
core.p: **Inbreeding** is breeding between **closely related individuals**. Selective breeding often involves inbreeding because the breeder wants to keep the desired alleles. Close relatives share many of the same alleles, so inbreeding **reduces the gene pool** and makes it more likely that two copies of a **harmful recessive allele** come together in an offspring. This leads to inherited defects and some breeds being prone to disease. The wider the gene pool the less likely this is.

bullets: Many alleles → more variation → more chance some individuals survive a new disease.
Few alleles → individuals are all equally **susceptible**.
Farmers sometimes keep **seed banks** and wild relatives to preserve alleles.
New pathogens can evolve to infect a widely grown variety, so breeding for resistance is a continuing process.
Reduced variation can limit future improvement because there are fewer alleles to select.
Link to natural selection: a population with low variation has less 'raw material' to adapt to environmental change.
Link to antibiotic resistance: farm animals bred in crowded conditions may need disease control, which can contribute to resistant bacteria if antibiotics are overused.
core.p: Selective breeding of crops or herds can produce populations that are **genetically very similar**. A population with many different alleles is more likely to contain some individuals that are **resistant** to a new disease, but a population that is almost genetically identical may have **no resistance at all**, so one disease can wipe out much of it. This is a major risk for modern agriculture where a few high-yielding varieties are grown over large areas. The Irish potato famine of the 1840s is often used as an example, where much of the crop was of very similar genetic type and potato blight devastated it.

bullets: Advantage: **increased yield** of milk, meat, eggs, grain, so more food for a growing population.
Advantage: crops with **disease resistance** reduce losses and pesticide use.
Advantage: **cheaper** and simpler technology than genetic engineering and widely accepted.
Disadvantage: **slow**, taking many generations.
Disadvantage: **inbreeding** and defects, which cause suffering or higher vet costs.
Disadvantage: **loss of variation** makes populations vulnerable to disease or climate change.
Disadvantage: may select for one feature at the cost of another (for example high yield but lower hardiness).
Ethics: debate about animal welfare, 'designer' pets, and whether humans should alter organisms for convenience.
Conclusion: it is valuable when managed carefully, for example avoiding closely related matings and preserving diversity.
core.h: Advantages and disadvantages: evaluating selective breeding
core.p: Evaluation questions (often 4 or 6 marks) want you to weigh benefits against drawbacks and reach a judgement. **Benefits** include higher yields, better quality, disease resistance and a more reliable food supply, using the natural variation already present and without direct changes to genes. **Drawbacks** include loss of genetic variation, inbreeding problems, slowness, and animal welfare concerns. A strong answer uses both sides then concludes.

bullets: Selective breeding: uses natural variation; slow; offspring differ from each other; limited to the species' own alleles.
Genetic engineering: **directly transfers genes** (for example from one species to another), faster, controversial.
Cloning: produces identical copies (for example by tissue culture or embryo transplants), reducing variation further.
Evolution link: it is an example of how a population's characteristics can change over generations.
Classification link: domestic animals remain the same species as wild ancestors if they can still produce fertile offspring.
Ecology link: farming practice and food security rely on these techniques.
Gene pool link: reduced diversity affects the ability to respond to change.
core.h: Links to genetic engineering, cloning and the wider topic
core.p: Selective breeding is the oldest of three ways of changing organisms. **Genetic engineering** changes the genome directly by moving a gene from one organism to another, which is faster and can transfer genes between species. **Cloning** produces genetically identical copies and is used to copy desirable individuals. Selective breeding relies on the **existing variation** in the species and takes many generations. Comparing all three is a common exam theme.

bullets: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.
Average change per generation = total change ÷ number of generations.
Look for whether the rise is steady, accelerating or levelling off.
A control (an unselected group kept in the same conditions) allows you to say the change is due to breeding.
Environmental effects (diet, climate) are confounding variables unless controlled.
Be careful with 'percentage' versus 'percentage points'.
Evaluate the data: how many animals, how many generations, repeated or not.
core.p: Data questions often show average yield per generation or per breed. A good approach is to describe the **trend**, quote values with units, and calculate **percentage change** or average change per generation. Remember that a rise may also be caused by improved feed or farming methods, not only breeding, so careful conclusions are needed. A graph that levels off may show that limits to the trait have been reached.

bullets: 'Describe how you could produce' (4 marks): select parents with the feature; breed them; select best offspring; repeat for many generations.
'Explain a problem of inbreeding': reduced gene pool / harmful recessive alleles more likely to pair / inherited disorders.
'Suggest why' disease resistance is important: less crop lost, less pesticide, more food.
'Evaluate' (6 marks): give two or more advantages and disadvantages and a final judgement.
'State' questions: one word or short phrase, such as 'inbreeding'.
Avoid saying the breeder 'changes the genes'; say the breeder **selects** organisms with the desired alleles.
Do not confuse with genetic engineering where genes are inserted.
core.h: Common exam contexts and model phrases
core.p: Typical questions ask you to **describe how** a breeder would produce an organism with a feature, to **explain** why a breed has health problems, or to **evaluate** the use of selective breeding. Use the key terms: **select**, **breed**, **offspring**, **repeat**, **many generations**, **gene pool**, **inbreeding**, **allele**. Always name the trait and link it to a benefit.

exam: 'Describe how selective breeding could be used to produce...' (4 marks): select parents with the feature → breed them → select best offspring → repeat over many generations. One mark each.
Always include the idea of **repeating over many generations** and **choosing the best offspring**.
Say what the feature is and why it is useful (for example 'high milk yield so more profit').
For 'explain why inbreeding is a problem': **reduces the gene pool**, **harmful recessive alleles** more likely to be inherited from both parents, so more **inherited disorders**.
For 'evaluate' (6 marks): two benefits, two drawbacks, link to ethics and reach a **judgement**; use 'however' to show balance.
Differentiate from **genetic engineering**: selective breeding uses natural variation and many generations, GE moves a gene directly.
Examples to quote: **disease-resistant crops**, **cows for milk**, **dogs with a gentle nature**, **large flowers**.
For data: calculate percentage change or average change per generation and show working.
Use scientific words: 'select', 'breed', 'offspring', 'alleles', 'inherited'; avoid 'make' or 'create' the gene.
If the question says 'explain', link a cause to its effect (because...).
Look at the number of marks: 2 marks = two points, 6 marks = a structured argument.

mistakes.r: The farmer selects cows with the desired alleles and breeds them; the genes are not directly altered (that is genetic engineering).
mistakes.w: The farmer changes the genes of the cows.

mistakes.r: Select and breed the best offspring over many generations.
mistakes.w: Breed the best animals together once.

mistakes.r: It uses alleles that already exist in the population; new alleles come from mutation.
Inbreeding makes it more likely that two copies of a harmful recessive allele are inherited, so defects appear; it does not cause mutations.
In selective breeding humans choose the parents for useful traits; in natural selection the environment selects for survival.
mistakes.w: Selective breeding is the same as natural selection.

mistakes.r: It takes many generations, so is slow, especially for animals that mature slowly.
It reduces variation (gene pool) because only a few individuals breed.
Domestic dog breeds are still one species since they can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Only if the trait is controlled by alleles that the parents pass on; offspring vary, so the best are chosen each time.
mistakes.w: All the offspring will have the trait if two parents have it.

summary: You must know that selective breeding (artificial selection) is humans breeding plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics, describe the repeated select-breed cycle, give examples such as disease-resistant crops, high-yield animals and gentle dogs, and explain the problem of inbreeding. It matters because it is used to produce most of our food and pets, and exams ask you to describe, explain and evaluate it.

terms.d: The process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics (artificial selection).
Another name for selective breeding, where humans rather than the environment choose which organisms breed.
Breeding between closely related individuals, which reduces the gene pool and increases the risk of inherited defects.
All the alleles in a population.
A different version of the same gene.
Differences between individuals in a population, caused by genes, the environment or both.
The range of different alleles present in a population.
A disease or condition caused by faulty alleles passed from parents to offspring.
A feature of an organism, such as milk yield or flower colour.
The amount of a useful product (for example milk, grain or fruit) produced.
The ability of an organism to avoid becoming ill when exposed to a pathogen.
Describes animals or plants kept or grown by humans.
An animal that has been selectively bred and whose ancestry is recorded.
Changing the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism.

worked.ans: Choose cows with high milk yield and a bull from a high-yielding line and breed them. From the offspring, select the ones with the highest milk yield and breed them together. Repeat this process over many generations so that more of the herd carry the alleles for high milk yield.
worked.q: A farmer wants to produce a herd of cattle that give a high milk yield. Describe how selective breeding could be used. (4 marks)
steps: Select the cows and bull that give/come from the highest milk yield.
Select the offspring (heifers) with the highest milk yield, as measured.

worked.ans: Pedigree dogs are bred from closely related individuals (inbreeding), which reduces the gene pool. This makes it more likely that a dog inherits two copies of a harmful recessive allele, so inherited disorders appear.
worked.q: Some pedigree dogs suffer from inherited health problems. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Breeders use closely related dogs: inbreeding.
Harmful recessive alleles more likely to be inherited from both parents.

worked.ans: 40% increase; 1.6 litres per cow per day per generation.
worked.q: Average milk yield of a herd rose from 20 litres per cow per day to 28 litres over 5 generations of selective breeding (illustrative data). Calculate the percentage increase and the mean increase per generation. (3 marks)
steps: Mean increase per generation = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6 litres per generation.
